sections.title: Chairman's Chat
sections.content:
Tam (AKA Glorious Leader) reports

How’s your assessment of risk!? Apparently in South Africa this is run of the mill stuff -  they’ve been doing this for about 20 years and they don’t understand the global outcry. Just another day living life to the full. In this instance it was to give the All Blacks a scare before the second test match in Cape Town. Had I been on the pitch, I think it would certainly have worked! All above board, planned, approved by the authorities, 3 massively experienced pilots in each cockpit, and clearly a spectacular success. Excellent, that’s ok then, everything went to plan, on the next event. Our sport is full of calculated risk taking. There was once a massively experienced paraglider pilot in the UK who’s party piece was to unclip from his harness on approach to landing, swoop in low and leap out of the harness leaving his wing to fly on by itself for a bit. Quite a spectacle, and always appreciated by an unsuspecting crowd. Eventually of course, it all went wrong and a sudden gust whisked him up to more height as he was jumping out of the harness - resulting in a broken back, and ego. On a SIV course I was on, the instructor told me he used to always finish flights with a spiral dive into a ground spiral.  Until one day he flew with someone who watched in admiration of his skill and then said his best mate used to do the same thing - until he was killed doing exactly the same thing as always only for something to go wrong in the last split second.  The difference to the exploits in our sport to the picture from Cape Town is of course that we aren’t risking the lives of 50,000 people other people who are in close proximity when we are at the point of most risk.It’s all very well us calculating our risk exposure and tolerance as we enjoy our sport, hopefully not increasing the risk for any third parties. But remember - just because it’s always worked before doesn’t mean it always will in the future. I think I’ll steer clear of attending any major sporting events in South Africa!

Fly safe everyone, hopefully see you at the camping week end

sections.title: Club Nights – 2026/2027
sections.content:
Mike Barker reports

Following the positive feedback from last season, we'll be continuing our revised club night format.

Join us from 7:00pm in the bar area of the Horse n Farrier in Otley for pre-drinks and parachat—a great opportunity for new members to meet fellow pilots and socialise before the evening begins. Presentations will start at 7:30pm in the function room and will last up to 90 minutes, including a refreshment break halfway through. Afterwards, there'll be plenty of time to catch up with friends, enjoy the live music downstairs, or head home if you've got a long drive or work the next day.

The Horse & Farrier kindly provides the function room free of charge, so please support them where you can, thank the staff, and treat the venue with courtesy and respect.

This year's programme has been put together with the aim of offering something for everyone—new pilots, rusty pilots, nervous pilots, and even the sky gods looking to sharpen their skills. All of the talks below are confirmed for the 2026/27 season, so pop the dates in your diary and come along!

Thursday 1st October

The Northern Challenge Series – Winter Edition
 An exciting new winter version of the Northern Challenge Series, designed to help keep both new and experienced pilots current and motivated throughout the quieter months.
With thanks to Ed Cleasby.

Thursday 5th November

British Accuracy Pilots Academy
 With recent discussions about landing incidents on social media, this is an excellent opportunity to improve your landing skills. Who knows—you might even be tempted to have a go at the competitions!
With thanks to Andy Shaw and the British Accuracy Cup.

Thursday 3rd December

AGM & Awards Night
 Our annual AGM, followed by the presentation of trophies and the ever-coveted DHPC mugs.
With thanks to the DHPC Committee.

Thursday 7th January

Sports Psychology for Paraglider Pilots
 Fear, anxiety and pressure are all part of flying in a harness supported by string attached to some nylon. This talk explores how these psychological demands affect us, how they manifest physiologically, and practical strategies for managing them. It will also cover improving decision-making, confidence, consistency and performance—for the sky gods among us as well!
With thanks to Michael Deaville, Sports Psychologist, Leeds Beckett University.

Thursday 4th February

Astronomy for Pilots (by popular demand!)
 Perfect for those bivvying out under the stars—or anyone who missed Brian Cox's Arena tour. A fascinating guide to the night sky, our solar system, and why we're all essentially made from stardust… or perhaps nuclear waste!
With thanks to Mike Barker (who claims to know more about this than paragliding!).

Thursday 4th March

SIV?! – Simulation d'Incident en Vol (simulation of in-flight incidents)
 A group discussion on SIV experiences, with pilots sharing lessons learned from their first course through to those with many SIVs under their wings. A chance to learn from others' experiences and ask plenty of questions.

Thursday 1st April

Video Night
 An informal evening reviewing real flying incidents captured on camera, covering take-offs, in-flight situations and landings. We'll draw on the themes from previous talks to discuss what happened, what can be learned, and how we can all become safer and more confident pilots. The emphasis is firmly on learning, improving and sharing experiences.
With thanks to the DHPC Committee.

Further details on each talk will be published closer to the dates:

My thanks in advance to all of our speakers for generously giving up their time to make this programme possible. I always welcome constructive feedback, so if you have any ideas, suggestions, or potential speakers for the 2027/28 season, please let me know!

See you on a hill,

Mike Barker
DHPC Social Secretary

sections.title: Coaching
sections.content:
Pete Logan, Chief Coach reports

It’s the Dales’ turn to run a coaching course this winter. Our club coaches are encouraged to brush up their skills every five years to help newly qualified and developing pilots become more confident in the air and stay safe whilst having fun. We have more than twenty coaches so do not be hesitant about getting in touch and arranging to meet on a hill to improve your flying or get your pilot tasks signed off.

So where are they?


Who are they?
Contact details are here - just log in to your Forum account or request one to be setup.

sections.title: The Baildon Sod
sections.content:
Pete Logan, reports

It was a double header of a night on the 12th August. The partial eclipse and, perhaps more importantly, 2026’s Baildon Sod. Here’s a few photographs…

Getting a decent view of the eclipse in the 200mm Schmidt-Cassegrain refractor.

Always plenty of launch help on hand.

Pound shop St Hilaire festival of flight at Baildon…

We had a hint of a westerly up until the eclipse which switched off and there was initially a requirement to get a clean launch and committed run in order to clear the bracken. Later that got easier after the Sod gods had been appeased by pilots sacrificed to the bracken and a light easterly breeze enabled much better launches but at the cost of overall distance.

Proving it’s all about technique, we had a couple of new fliers visiting from the Sussex Downs. Sally couldn’t have been much more than 50kg which means you’ve got to be flying by the bracken not “bull in a China shopping” your way through. She managed the far side of the golf course.


Chris Fountain won this year, a first at the Sod for him, he’s only been flying for 30 years ;-) Close joint seconds were new pilot Adam Westhead and Pete Logan. Possibly others but I’d given up counting by then.

sections.title: Summerbridge
sections.content:
Pete D chronicles his exploits on 10th August

By rights I should have been kicking the dirt on Summerbridge cricket pitch before half-past two, cursing my inability to read the sky, and all those around, animate or inanimate, in the air or on the ground, before consoling myself with an ice cream or pint, or both.  It wasn’t even my first mistake of the day; I had slope-landed a whole six minutes after my initial take-off and then tried not to watch the gaggle climb out and leave me for dead.

However, this time the sun gods intervened and a small bubble 114 metres above an unlikely lee side slope gained me 100 precious vertical metres.  I promptly lost this again but found the next bubble kicking off Summerbridge itself.  With 200 more metres in the bag, I was in a better place when this bubble was depleted, or I lost it, and could reach the sunny into-wind slopes above.  And so, five scratty climbs later, I was back in the game at the dizzying heights of 1300 English metres.

Determined to put this new-found fortune to good use, I resolved to fly like a more accomplished pilot, and to get the best out of the remaining day.  The cirrus top cover did not make things easy, but I found a welcome ally in Simon Hulme, who fresh from his own bottom-feeding-in-Nidderdale experience, was also struggling to get back to base.

We bisected Harrogate and its less pretentious neighbour, much to the chagrin of Alex Colbeck who could see us from his office window, and then it was time for the next big decision of the day.  Clearly the giddy long-distance goals in Lincolnshire were out of the question, put paid by the lack of tailwind and the encroaching top-cover from the south of west.

The sky looked best further north in the Vale of York, and the light wind had convinced many of the lead gaggle to take that approach.  The second-best option, sky-wise that is, was to head east towards York, following in the erstwhile turns of Pete Logan.  However, I have been there before, more than once, and on days with a forecast significant sea breeze, getting much past York is doomed.

RASP forecast boundary layer average wind for 17:00 - York already engulfed

So it was, I took the lonely option of heading east of south, under the increasingly cirrus-laden sky, paralleling Leeds Bradford airspace and aiming for gap between that and the mighty Leeds East aerodrome traffic zone.  Heading 180 degrees to the best-looking sky was not completely un-joined-up thinking, well not in my mind anyway; there were still cumulus clouds under the cirrus, albeit not as impressive as those earlier in the flight, and it should keep one out of the sea breeze for longer.

This plan was actually going rather swimmingly until approaching Knottingley where the now not so insignificant wind aloft was backing from west to south of west, the top cover was thickening up, and the last remaining ragged cumulus markers to the south had evaporated.  I took the opportunity to climb back to base, whilst admiring the meanders in the Aire, and changed tack for Doncaster.  This should have been eminently achievable from my soaring position 1900 metres above the river, but only if one ignored or disbelieved multiple instrument wind widgets.

Aire meanders - 17:20

And so it was, 100 kilometres in the bag, I found myself circling over the town of Askern, lacking the requisite enthusiasm for a few extra kilometres just to land closer but still shy of Donny, and set up for a landing facing east at a different parched cricket pitch.  Had I known of course that the bus would drive right past the scheduled stop, completely ignoring myself, I would have carried on anyway as the Uber to the once famous LNER hub would have been two pounds cheaper.

Sky fix satiated for the time being, all that was left was for a quick endorphin hit cycling out to collect the abandoned car.  All in all, a grand day out in God’s own county, despite my attempts to thwart it.

Route, airspace and altitude - note: shows GPS not barometric altitude

sections.title: Invite to the Farmers’ Dinner - October 17th.
sections.content:
Tam reports

The time is approaching for the annual Farmers’ Dinner where we treat “our farmers” to a slap up meal at The Knights Table, Stainforth, near Settle - an establishment run by club member Chris Maudsley. As you probably know, unlike many clubs, particularly down south, we pay very in site fees each year.  Instead we invite all the farmers/landowners who we rely on for access to our sites to this meal each year. Many don’t come, but quite a few do and it’s always a convivial evening and they love to hear of the antics we get up using their land - it’s very good PR for the club. Several of the committee go each year. Members and partners are always welcome too. It’s a pretty informal affair, no need for black tie or anything!

The menu for the coming event, on October 17th, is below, including costs. If you would like to go please let Dave Bradwell (treasurer@dhpc.org.uk) know who’s coming, and your menu choices, and pay the appropriate amount into the club bank account: DHPC, Sort code: 08-92-99, A/c# 65335930. It would be great to see more members there!

sections.title: Paragliding Tow Conversion at Rutland Airpsorts
sections.content:
Simon Hulme reports

August was ushered in with another awesome weekend weather forecast……at least for the south-west anyway.  A group of Dales XC ninjas were heading south on the Thursday night ready for some big distance flights from both Worcester Beacon and Llangorse.  I tagged along on Saturday hoping to learn by osmosis from some of the best pilots in the UK.  But as with much of my first year of XC it was a bit of hit mixed with a lot of miss.  So, whilst the ninjas hit 200+ km for the second day on the bounce, I was forced to slope land after 30 minutes as it was getting pretty unpleasant with 20 or so pilots desperately scratching whilst they waited for the next cycle.  As I have found out all too often this summer the difference between barely enough lift and blown out on the hill can be minutes few.  2 hours para-waiting, talking para-bollox and an air ambulance for a braver/more foolish soul, later we retired from Worcester Beacon
 
Sunday was looking a little more challenging for big distances flights so after back-to-back 200s some decided on a well-earned day of rest the others headed to the Peak District.  I on the other hand, having spent Saturday sat frustrated on the hill, was off to Rutland, the UK’s smallest county for a paragliding tow conversion with Rutland Airports based out of what was once RAF North Luffenham but is now a disused airfield with an Army barracks attached.  
 
So why did I decide to do the tow conversion and is it for everyone?  TBH it was all a little bit last minute and not at all thought through in advance, which is most unlike me.  I know Rutland well having flown the Tornado from RAF Cottesmore, which is just a few miles away across Rutland Water so quite fancied a trip down memory lane.  There had been chat earlier in the week about heading there on the Sunday anyway to fly a triangle as RASP was looking good and winds were light.  I had messaged Mick Roche the Chief Instructor in the extremely remote hope of blagging a conversion course and as it turned out there were 19 people on the list ahead of me, but even so they were struggling to get the 3 people they needed to run the course that was needed on Sunday to facilitate a BHPA assessed instructor upgrade.  So, 3 days from first contact I was all ready to go for my tow conversion – zero prep but I was there, wide eyed and raring to go.
 
The first thing to note is that Rutland Airsports is affiliated to the MOD and as a club 50% of members must be serving military personnel – this is a condition of getting free access to a military airfield but means the club is currently closed to new members.  They can still run conversion courses, but post qualification full club members get priority, which means on great flying days non-members probably aren’t going to get a spot, especially at weekends.  The second thing to note is that even though the Club is run by volunteers it does have a bit of a ‘military feel’ about it …a bit less chilled than most things paragliding, and they run a tight ship.  I don’t mean that as a criticism, I felt quite at home, and the quality of instruction during the morning’s ground school was great with a solid emphasis on both technique and emergencies.  That was a good job as it will become clear.
 
The tow conversion entails about 3 hours of ground school and all being well 10 tow flights for a hill qualified pilot with CP + 10 hours.  It wouldn’t be the BHPA course without an exam so remember to RFTQ. It’ll cost you about £90 for the conversion, which I thought was great VFM and then you’ll then have to pay £20 to the BHPA to have your licence amended.  Post qualification each tow costs £2 and day membership is £12 – spoiler alert you may need more than 1 tow to bag a good thermal.
 
I’m not going to try to offer ‘a how to of tow paragliding’ – I’ve done the conversion and an additional 6 tows, so I’m not qualified but I’ll offer a few thoughts/observations, which you can feel free to totally ignore:
 
-  If they offer you a tandem tow then take it – it will demystify your first solo flight considerably.  
 
-  I didn’t find the tow launch too daunting, the wing is definitely a long way back behind you, akin to what you’d see in a rapid exit from a spiral dive but with less drama than a spiral dive.  It was a bit rock and roll on the tow once the thermals started to kick off – you can certainly feel the wing surge when you hit one.
 
-  The way the wing behaves on the tow and particularly when you are not tracking to the winch took me some time to get my head around during the ground school – a bit more prep pre course would have helped!!!  It was a bit more obvious once I’d seen it airborne, but it still took several flights to nail the scan and keep tracking to the winch, particularly towards the top of the tow.  Don’t worry - there is plenty of well-timed coaching delivered over the radio to keep you on the straight and narrow.    
 
- make sure you are happy with the emergency procedures during the ground school because they can and do happen.   You will normally be required to practice some simulated emergencies during the conversion, but I had a genuine tow failure to release, an inadvertent reserve deployment, and a winch stall at about 30 feet on my first trip back post conversion course.  The BHPA Technical Officer was onsite for my failure to separate, and an occurrence report was submitted.  A post flight examination of the Gin tow bridle I was using showed a clear manufacturing build quality fault that led to the failed release. This problem had been seen before at Rutland Airsports and Gin had been notified but chose to do nothing.  The inadvertent reserve deployment was a bit of bad luck but easily avoided – I am right-handed so have the tow release set for my right hand and had quickly developed the habit of letting the tow cable sit to the right of my pod harness.  On my final qualification tow, I pulled the bridle release and very shortly after felt a strong pull around my neck – it was the most discombobulated I have been in the air for many years.  With 2020 hindsight and having watched several briefs on reserve deployments during SIV courses the down planning wing and pull at my shoulders should have been obvious. However, I hadn’t pulled the reserve handle, it must have been snagged somehow by the tow bridle or tow cable during the release, and all I could think was how did the tow cable get caught around my neck?  I know crazy how the mind works.
 
A well-timed call of ‘depower the wing’ from the coach over the radio snapped me back into reality.  It took a good deal of effort to depower the wing but that sorted the rate of descent and I had a good 10-15 look around and prepare for the PLF, which at 115kg under a 140kg square reserve was very gentle.  I had turned down the opportunity to practice a reserve throw during my SIV training but now I’ve seen it/felt it I’ll be better prepared in future. Oh, and how to reduce the chance of inadvertent reserve pull – simples! I now make sure the tow cable sits to the left of my pod and the tow bridle sits across the top of the pod.  The tow cable goes nowhere near my reserve handle, and it is easier to see the bridle split into its 2 halves.
 
I’ll leave it to the chief coach or one of the other XC ninjas to talk about the overseas opportunities that a tow qualification opens up for you, but that wasn’t the motivation for me, at least not in the near term.  I have plenty to keep me busy developing my XC skills in the UK and having an extra arrow in the quiver will certainly help with XC opportunities from a different site in the UK.  I’d highly recommend Rutland Airsports – it’s a very well-run club with a bunch of great people.  I’ll be joining as soon as membership opens again.

Pete Logan:

Although I’d not gotten my tow conversion for the purpose of going abroad, it was one less thing to do ahead of going and flying the Sertão in the NE of Brazil when a bunch of us did decide to. It’s an arid mix of mainly flatland and jaw dropping hill country. Miles from anywhere you’re likely to have heard of, huge in scale and the place where, about this time each year, pilots gather to use the reliable easterlies to fly their biggest distances.

These easterlies are also strong and you’ll want to be getting off the ground as early as possible to maximise your distance. To help with both of these factors, small strip airfields are used to tow launch pilots to 700m and above as early as 6:45am. To speed up turn around, trucks with payout winches are used. For our airfield on the outskirts of the town Assu we were laying out on a small piece of tarpaulin with helpers, waiting for the wind to drop enough and then popping the wing up, checking, turning and taking tension all in about three seconds.  

Two wide postage stamp for launch.

The truck drivers know what they’re doing, and it’s a gentle payout to start off, just to get some length on the line which helps in avoiding lock outs when the tension increases. For the first ten seconds you’re barely climbing or going forward and then it’s time for the tension to ratchet. After this gentle phase the wing will drop back in the oncoming wind and on the strongest days the vario will scream at 4up and you barely move forward of the launch point as the truck pays out, using a balance of forward speed and brake on the pay out drum.

Chris launching with the truck a fair distance away, paying out line.

On the way up there’s buffeting from the small thermals which I was using the B lines to smooth out so the wing didn’t drag more than necessary. And then the truck reaches the end of the strip and and does a 180 to signal release time. There’s a lot of weight on the line so you don’t always get a clean separation which can lead to some thrutching about as the wing settles in pitch. But at the end of all that you're left at 1000m and just the lightest of thermals to survive with. You need to go from high adrenaline to Zen like mincing in another few seconds. Now you just have a VERY long day ahead of you. Land by time is 5:45pm!

I would wholeheartedly second Simon’s opinion on expanding your possibilities and capabilities. Mick Roche at Rutland runs a tight operation and engenders trust as a tow conversion instructor. He’s also a very ordered ex RAF type, and the look of disappointment on his face when I inadvertently turned up in a pair of Crocs to get my conversion 😬

Me above the land ‘o lakes approaching the monoliths of Quixadá.
